en: This section tells how these shores and also these islands were found. These coasts are called the shores of Antilia. They were discovered in the year 896 of the Arab calendar. But it is reported that a Genoese infidel named Colombo discovered these places. A book had fallen into the hands of this Colombo, and he found written in it that at the far end of the Western Sea there were coasts and islands and all kinds of metals and precious stones. Having studied this book, he explained these matters to the chiefs of Genoa and said, "Give me two ships, let me go and find these places." They said, "O foolish man, can an end or a limit be found to the Western Sea? Its mists are full of darkness." Seeing that no help came from the Genoese, Colombo went to the Bey of Spain and told his tale in detail. In short, the Bey of Spain gave him two ships, well equipped, and said, "O Colombo, if it happens as you say, I will make you admiral of that country." Advancing four thousand miles, he saw an island; but little by little the North Star was veiled, and he said the stars in that region are arranged differently. The islanders shot arrows and would not let them land; the men and women shoot arrows tipped with fishbone, and the whole population goes naked. They neared another island where there were great snakes, and avoided it. The people gave them glass beads and fish; they saw gold on a woman's arm, and traded beads for gold, for there were gold mines in the mountains. They carried two natives back to the Bey of Spain. The coasts and islands on this map are taken from Colombo's map.

This section shows in what way this map was drawn. In this age no one has seen a map like this. The hand of this poor man drew it from about twenty charts and world maps — these are charts drawn in the days of Alexander, Lord of the Two Horns, which show the inhabited quarter of the world, the Arabs naming such charts "Jaferiye." From eight such Jaferiyes, and from one Arab map of Hind, and from four newly drawn Portuguese maps which show the lands of Sind, Hind and China geometrically, and also from a map drawn by Columbus in the western region, I have extracted it. By reducing all these maps to one scale, this final form was arrived at, so that this map is as accurate and reliable for the Seven Seas as the maps of those lands are to seamen.

This map was drawn by the poor man Piri, son of Hajji Mehmed, nephew of Kemal Reis — may God have mercy on them both — in the town of Gelibolu (Gallipoli), in the month of Muharram of the year 919, that is, between the 9th of March and the 7th of April of the year 1513.

This sea is called the Western Sea, but the Frank sailors call it the Mare d'Espagna, which means the Sea of Spain. Until now it was known by these names, but Colombo, who opened up this sea, and the Portuguese infidels who opened the region of Hind, have agreed to give this sea a new name. They named it Ovo Sano (Oceano) — that is, a sound egg. Before this it was thought the sea had no end or limit, that at its far side was darkness. Now they have seen that this sea is girded by a coast and is like a lake, so they called it Ovo Sano.

It is said that in ancient times a priest named Sanvolrandan (Santo Brandan) travelled the Seven Seas. The above-mentioned islands lie upon a great fish. They thought it land and lit a fire upon this fish. When the fish's back began to burn it plunged into the sea; they re-embarked their boats and fled to the ship. This event is not mentioned by the Portuguese infidels. It is taken from the ancient Mappae Mundi.

The Portuguese infidels do not go west of here. All that side belongs entirely to Spain. They have agreed that a line two thousand miles to the western side of the Strait of Gibraltar be taken as a boundary. The Portuguese do not cross to that side; but the Hind side and the southern side belong to the Portuguese.

This region is known as the province of Antilia. It is on the side where the sun sets. They say there are four kinds of parrots — white, red, green and black. The people eat the flesh of parrots, and their headdress is made entirely of parrots' feathers. There is a stone here resembling black touchstone, which the people use instead of the axe; it is very hard. We saw that stone.

On the way to the province of Hind a Portuguese ship met a contrary wind from the shore. Driven by a storm in a southern direction, they saw a shore opposite and steered towards it. They saw that these places were good anchorages and inhabited. They threw anchor and went ashore in boats. They saw people walking naked, who shot arrows tipped with fishbone. They stayed eight days, trading by signs. The ship returned to Portugal, where on arrival it gave information about these shores in detail. Thus they were discovered.

And these four ships are Portuguese ships. Their shape is drawn here. They travelled from the western land to the point of Abyssinia in order to reach India; they held towards Shuluk. The distance across this gulf is 4,200 miles.
To these small islands they have given the name Undizi Vergine — that is to say, the Eleven Virgins.
A Genoese cog coming from Flanders was caught in a storm. Driven by the storm it came upon these islands, and in this way these islands became known.
And this island they call the Island of Antilia. There are many monsters and parrots, and much logwood. It is not inhabited.
Having met a storm, this caravel — named Nicola Giuvan — came upon this island. On it there are many oxen with one horn, and for this reason they call it the Isle of Vacca, which means Ox Island.

The admiral of this caravel is named Messir Anton the Genoese, but he grew up in Portugal. One day the caravel met a storm and was driven upon this island. He found much ginger here, and has written about these islands.

This ship was driven onto these shores by a storm; its name was Nicola di Giuvan. On his map it is written that these rivers, for the most part, carry gold in their beds. When the water had gone down they collected much gold dust from the sand.
In the mountains of this land there are beasts like this, and on the shore many men; and the gold of its mine has no end.
These monsters are seven spans long. Between their eyes there is a distance of one span. But they are harmless creatures.
In this spot there are oxen with one horn, and also monsters of this shape.
This land is inhabited, and its people are plentiful.
This is the ship from Portugal which met a storm and reached this land. The details are written on the margin of this map.
And in this country there are said to be white-haired monsters of this shape, and also six-horned oxen. The Portuguese infidels have drawn them on their maps.
These islands are deserted, but there are many spices.

This country is a waste. Everything is in ruin, and it is said that large snakes are found here. For this reason the Portuguese infidels did not land on these shores, which are also said to be very hot.
This country is inhabited. The entire population goes naked.
There is a red dye called Vakami; it is not seen on the far side, being very distant.
It is related by the Portuguese infidels that here the shortest day is two hours and the longest twenty-two. The day is very warm, and in the night there is much dew.
…on this shore a tower… in this climate gold… taking a rope… it is said they measured…
